summary: Describes F-RTO, a sender-only algorithm for detecting spurious retransmission timeouts in TCP and SCTP. A spurious timeout causes unnecessary resending of data, which hurts performance. F-RTO needs no TCP options. The document is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: F-RTO helps a TCP sender detect when its retransmission timer expired even though the original data was only delayed. The sender uses later acknowledgements to decide whether to stop retransmitting or return to normal timeout recovery.

questions: what is a spurious retransmission timeout
subtitle: A sender-side algorithm for detecting when a retransmission timeout was unnecessary.

tldr.problem: A retransmission timeout can expire even when packets were delayed rather than lost. Conventional recovery may then resend data that the receiver already got.
tldr.mechanism: F-RTO retransmits the first unacknowledged segment, then observes acknowledgements and may send new data. If later acknowledgements cover data not retransmitted after the timeout, it identifies the timeout as spurious.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4138 defines an Experimental detection algorithm for TCP and SCTP. It was updated by RFC 5682; this memo does not define the response to a detected spurious timeout.

today: RFC 4138 is an Experimental memo and was updated by RFC 5682. It describes detection, not the response to a spurious timeout.

sections.title: When a Timeout Is a False Alarm
sections.content:
A TCP retransmission timeout (RTO) tells a sender to treat unacknowledged data as lost. The sender reduces its congestion window and retransmits data using slow start. A timeout is spurious if it would have been avoided by waiting longer for an acknowledgement.

Delay spikes can result from a mobile hand-off, competing traffic or loss and retransmission at a reliable link layer. When the original data later generates acknowledgements, a conventional sender may retransmit a whole window unnecessarily. F-RTO changes sender behavior only after an RTO and does not require TCP options.
sections.plainLanguage: A timeout can happen because an acknowledgement is late, even when the data arrived. The sender may then repeat data that the receiver already has.

sections.title: The Basic F-RTO Steps
sections.content:
When the RTO expires, the sender retransmits the first unacknowledged segment, sets SpuriousRecovery to FALSE and records the highest sequence number sent in recover. On the first acknowledgement, a duplicate ACK, an ACK at or beyond recover, or an ACK that does not cover all data retransmitted in the first step sends the sender back to conventional recovery.

If the first ACK advances the window below recover, the sender sends up to two previously unsent segments and waits for a second ACK. A duplicate second ACK leads to conventional recovery. If the second ACK advances the window by acknowledging data that was not retransmitted after the timeout, the sender declares the timeout spurious.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender first repeats one segment, then checks the next acknowledgements. It calls the timeout spurious only when an acknowledgement proves that data sent before the timeout arrived without being retransmitted.

sections.title: Why F-RTO Uses Cautious Checks
sections.content:
Duplicate acknowledgements may indicate packet loss, so they do not provide enough evidence to declare a timeout spurious. The sender also requires the first ACK to cover all data retransmitted in the first step; otherwise, a receiver acknowledging incomplete data could mislead it.

F-RTO can miss a spurious timeout when reordering or duplication affects the segment that triggered it, or when the timeout occurs during fast recovery. In those cases it uses conventional recovery. After detection, a separate response algorithm decides how congestion-control state should change.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender treats uncertain acknowledgements as possible evidence of loss and returns to conventional recovery. Detecting a false alarm and deciding how to respond are separate tasks.

sections.title: The SACK-Enhanced Variant
sections.content:
When TCP Selective Acknowledgment (SACK) is enabled, a sender may use the SACK-enhanced F-RTO variant. SACK blocks identify received data more precisely and can reveal that data sent before the timeout arrived, even when duplicate ACKs occur.

The variant still retransmits the first unacknowledged segment and checks subsequent acknowledgements. The sender returns to conventional recovery when the acknowledgements do not provide sufficient evidence; when a later acknowledgement confirms data not retransmitted after the timeout, it declares the timeout spurious. The RFC advises against using this variant when the sender was already in SACK loss recovery at timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: SACK gives the sender a more detailed report of which data arrived. That extra information can help identify a false timeout when packets arrive out of order.

sections.title: Use with SCTP and Security Notes
sections.content:
The algorithm can also be applied to the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP), which has similar retransmission and acknowledgement behavior. The RFC recommends the SACK-based variant for SCTP because SCTP uses selective acknowledgements. For multi-homed SCTP associations, it recommends conservative congestion-control actions when retransmissions use alternative addresses.

A receiver could try to mislead a sender into increasing its congestion window by acknowledging data it did not receive or delaying an acknowledgement. The RFC explains why the first approach is unlikely to help and recommends caution when a timeout occurs during fast recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP has similar timers and acknowledgements, so the same detection idea can apply. A sender should remain cautious because false reports from a receiver could affect its sending rate.
